title: Graph theory
summary: Graphs, adjacency matrices and walks, Eulerian and Hamiltonian routes, minimum spanning trees, the Chinese postman problem and bounds for the travelling salesman problem.

keyterms.definition: A set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges.
The number of edges meeting at a vertex; the sum of degrees is twice the number of edges.
A graph with no loops and no multiple edges between the same pair of vertices.
Every pair of vertices is joined by exactly one edge; Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges.
A matrix whose (i, j) entry is the number of edges from vertex i to vertex j.
A sequence of linked vertices; Aⁿ gives the number of walks of length n.
A closed route using every edge exactly once; exists when all degrees are even.
A closed route visiting every vertex exactly once.
A tree connecting all n vertices with n − 1 edges and the least total weight (Kruskal or Prim).
Finding the shortest closed route that travels every edge at least once.
Finding the shortest Hamiltonian cycle; bounded above by nearest neighbour and below by deleted vertex.

questions.text: A graph has 7 edges. The sum of the degrees of its vertices is ___.
questions.explanation: Each edge adds 1 to the degree at each end, so the sum is 2 × 7.

questions.statement: A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree.
questions.explanation: Each visit enters and leaves a vertex, using edges in pairs.

questions.prompt: How many edges does the complete graph K₅ have?
A connected graph has exactly two odd vertices, P and Q. Which is true?
options: It has an Eulerian trail from P to Q but no Eulerian circuit
questions.explanation: A trail can start and end at the two odd vertices.

questions.prompt: For adjacency matrix A, the (i, j) entry of A³ gives:
options: the shortest distance from i to j
the number of walks of length 3 from i to j
the number of edges in the graph
questions.explanation: Matrix powers count walks of that length.

questions.statement: A Hamiltonian cycle uses every edge exactly once.
questions.explanation: That describes an Eulerian circuit; a Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once.

questions.prompt: Match each route type to its rule.

pairs.right: closed path returning to its start

questions.explanation: Each type is more restrictive than a walk.

options: Every pair of vertices is joined
No loops and no multiple edges
questions.explanation: Simple graphs have at most one edge between any pair and no loops.

questions.text: A graph in which every pair of vertices is joined by exactly one edge is called ___.

questions.prompt: The adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is always:
questions.explanation: An edge from i to j is also an edge from j to i.

options: choosing the shortest edge in the whole graph
questions.explanation: Kruskal adds edges in order of weight; Prim grows from a chosen vertex.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Kruskal’s algorithm in order.
items: List the edges in increasing order of weight
Add the next shortest edge that does not form a cycle
Stop when n − 1 edges are included
questions.explanation: Rejecting cycle-forming edges keeps the result a tree.

questions.text: A spanning tree on n vertices has ___ edges.
questions.explanation: Any tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.

questions.statement: If every vertex has even degree, the Chinese postman route length equals the total weight of the edges.
questions.explanation: An Eulerian circuit exists, so no edge needs repeating.

questions.prompt: A network has total edge weight 52 and two odd vertices A and D. The shortest path from A to D has weight 7. Find the shortest Chinese postman route.
In the travelling salesman problem, the nearest neighbour algorithm gives:
questions.explanation: It gives a real cycle, so the optimum cannot be longer.

questions.statement: The deleted vertex algorithm gives an upper bound for the travelling salesman problem.
questions.explanation: It gives a lower bound: residual MST weight plus the two shortest edges from the deleted vertex.

questions.prompt: Match each problem to its method.

pairs.left: Connect all towns with least cable
Travel along every street and return
Visit every city once and return
Quick upper bound for the shortest tour

questions.explanation: Edges matter for the postman; vertices matter for the salesman.

questions.prompt: A network has total weight 80 and odd vertices A, B, C, D. Pairings: AB + CD = 9, AC + BD = 7, AD + BC = 11. Find the shortest Chinese postman route.
Deleted vertex gives a lower bound of 40 and nearest neighbour a tour of 46. The optimal tour length T satisfies:
questions.explanation: The optimum lies between the lower and upper bounds.
